sections.title: 7. How to Approach Any Knapsack Problem

blocks.text: The Knapsack pattern is one of the most important families in dynamic programming. Once you recognise it, a huge number of problems that look unrelated suddenly become the same problem wearing different clothes.

The core question is always the same: you have a set of items, each with a cost, and a limited budget. You must choose a subset of items to maximise value (or reach a target) without going over the budget.

blocks.caption: For each item you choose to take it or skip it, and keep the better outcome
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406553816-561791264.png
Imagine a thief with a bag that can hold at most W kilograms. In front of them are items, each with a weight and a value. They want to walk away with the most valuable haul the bag can carry.
That single story is the classic knapsack problem. Every knapsack variation reduces to the same tension: each item costs something from a limited budget, and you want the best total outcome.

items: A limited capacity or budget (weight, money, time)
A set of items, each consuming some of that budget
Each item gives some value or contributes to a goal
Choose the best subset that fits inside the budget

blocks.text:
The key signal:

If a problem says "pick some items so their total cost stays within a limit while optimising a value," you are almost certainly looking at knapsack.
Knapsack comes in two main flavours, and knowing which one you have decides the whole solution.
0/1 Knapsack
Each item exists once. For every item you make a binary choice: take it or leave it. This is why it is called 0/1. Subset sum, partition, and target sum problems are all 0/1 knapsack in disguise.
Unbounded Knapsack
Each item can be used as many times as you like. Coin change and rod cutting are unbounded knapsack, because you can reuse the same coin or cut repeatedly.
The two differ by a single detail in the code: the direction in which you loop over the capacity. That one line is the whole difference.
Let us define the state. Let dp[i][w] be the best value we can achieve using the first i items with a capacity of exactly w.
For each item we face the take-or-skip decision. If we skip item i, the answer is whatever we had without it. If we take it, we add its value and reduce the remaining capacity by its weight.

blocks.caption: Each cell is the better of skipping the item or taking it
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406553817-864922732.png
This gives the transition below. We simply keep the larger of the two options.

codes.cpp:
// dp[i][w] = best value from first i items with capacity w
dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w];                     // skip item i
if (wt[i - 1] <= w)                           // can we fit it?
    dp[i][w] = max(dp[i][w],
                   dp[i - 1][w - wt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1]); // take it
codes.python:

blocks.text: Putting the transition inside two loops, over items and over capacities, gives the classic table solution. The answer sits in the bottom-right corner.
This runs in O(n x W) time and space, where n is the number of items and W is the capacity.
Notice that row i only ever looks at row i minus one. We never need the whole table at once, just the previous row. That lets us collapse the 2D table into a single 1D array.
The one subtlety: for 0/1 knapsack we loop capacity from high to low, so each item is used at most once. For unbounded knapsack we loop low to high, which lets an item be reused.

codes.python:
# 0/1 knapsack in O(W) space
def knapsack(W, wt, val):
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)
    for i in range(len(wt)):
        for w in range(W, wt[i] - 1, -1):          # high to low: use each item once
            dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i])
    return dp[W]

blocks.text:
Remember the loop direction:

0/1 knapsack loops capacity high to low. Unbounded knapsack loops low to high. Flip that one loop and you switch between the two flavours.
Most knapsack interview problems never mention a bag at all. Learning to translate them into knapsack is the real skill.

items: Subset Sum: can any subset add up to a target? Value equals weight, ask if the target is reachable.
Partition Equal Subset Sum: split the array into two equal halves, which is subset sum for half the total.
Target Sum: assign plus or minus signs to reach a target, which rearranges into a subset sum.
Coin Change: fewest coins to make an amount, an unbounded knapsack minimising count.
Rod Cutting: maximise revenue from cutting a rod, an unbounded knapsack over lengths.

blocks.text: They differ only in what the "weight", the "value", and the "goal" map to. The machinery underneath does not change.

content.title: 7. How to Approach Any Knapsack Problem

blocks.text: When you suspect knapsack, walk through these steps and the solution usually falls out.

items: Identify the budget: what limited resource are you spending (weight, money, count)?
Identify the items and what each one costs from that budget.
Decide the flavour: is each item used once (0/1) or unlimited (unbounded)?
Define the state as dp indexed by items processed and budget remaining.
Write the take-or-skip transition and pick the better option.
Optimise the 2D table down to 1D once it works, minding the loop direction.

blocks.text: Get comfortable with this checklist and the entire knapsack family becomes one pattern you already know.
